## How close are groceries without a car?

A supermarket can be close by car and difficult to reach on foot. For Day 9's Urban-rural theme, I followed that difference across Hamilton and Clermont counties: Cincinnati and its surrounding neighbourhoods, suburban retail corridors, and the rural eastern fringe. Both maps use the same geography and five- and ten-minute travel budgets. The question is whether a trip can reach at least one included store.

The store inventory contains 90 selected locations inside the study area: 68 in Hamilton County and 22 in Clermont. Nearby destinations outside the counties also contribute. Excluding a supermarket just across a county or state line would create an artificial access gap.

## Method

I selected SNAP-authorized retailers classified as **Supermarket** or **Super Store**, excluding Costco and Sam's Club membership formats. This is a declared supermarket inventory, not every place that sells food. Smaller groceries, specialty shops, farmers markets and convenience stores are outside it. The [store table](stores.csv) and [exclusions](excluded-retailers.csv) preserve that choice.

The routing experiment uses **inbound isochrones** from [Valhalla](https://valhalla.github.io/valhalla/api/isochrone/): areas from which a store can be reached within the time budget. Direction matters on one-way streets. I requested each destination separately with `reverse = true`, retained smaller components, repaired invalid geometry where needed, and combined the resulting polygons locally for each mode and time band. The published map renders offline from those saved reductions.

Walking uses a 5.1 km/h baseline. Driving uses static road speeds with live and predicted traffic speed sources disabled; parking search, the walk from a parking space, and live closures are excluded. Source points snap to an eligible network location. The [snap table](store-snaps.csv) records those offsets; this is access to the modelled network location, not a timed walk through the store's front door.

Destinations within 25 km of the study area supply driving catchments, and those within 2 km supply walking catchments. The acquisition script checks the source envelope and records every requested store/mode pair. Contours are generalized at ten metres, so their filled interiors are approximate envelopes rather than a guarantee that every property inside them is accessible.

## Data & provenance

Store locations come from the [USDA SNAP Retailer Locator](https://www.fns.usda.gov/snap/retailer-locator), retrieved November 12, 2026. Authorization and store type do not establish opening hours, prices, product quality or cultural suitability. The source can also miss a relevant retailer or retain an outdated location.

The pink food-desert flags are a historical layer: USDA's **2019 vehicle-based low-income and low-access measure**, from the [Food Access Research Atlas](https://ers.usda.gov/data-products/food-access-research-atlas/update-and-revision-history). It flags 63 tracts here, 59 in Hamilton and four in Clermont. Its store directory is from 2019, income and vehicle estimates from the 2014–18 ACS, and tract geometry from the 2010 Census. These flags are not a current designation or recalculated routing results. Numbered examples identify tracts within Westwood, Avondale, Lincoln Heights, and Goshen, Batavia, Monroe and Ohio townships, rather than labelling whole places. The [callout table](callout-selections.csv) links each name to a tract; names were checked against Census place/township boundaries and [Cincinnati statistical neighbourhood approximations](https://data.cincinnati-oh.gov/dataset/Cincinnati-Statistical-Neighborhood-Approximations/i9zh-juvu).

The [2020 urban-area footprint](https://tigerweb.geo.census.gov/arcgis/rest/services/TIGERweb/Urban/MapServer) and county boundaries come from Census TIGERweb. The map uses NAD83 / UTM zone 16N. Routing uses OpenStreetMap via the FOSSGIS-hosted Valhalla service; map data © [OpenStreetMap contributors](https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright), under ODbL. The [acquisition script](acquire-data.R), [request manifest](routing-manifest.csv) and [source snapshot](source-snapshot.json) preserve inputs, assumptions and SHA-256 fingerprints. The [renderer](render-map.R) makes no network requests.

## What I learned

Food access is a relationship between a destination, a route, a mode and the resources available to make the trip. A driving catchment says little about access for a household without a car. The historical outlines help frame that question, but this map does not identify today's food deserts or measure household food insecurity. Transit, delivery, smaller retailers, cost and store hours could all change the practical picture.

**Alt text:** Walking and driving supermarket catchments across Hamilton and Clermont counties, with an urban–rural backdrop and separately labelled historical USDA food-access tracts, with numbered examples named in the key.
